input.question: How closely and with how much detail could astronomers see Jupiter in the 17th century?
input.ground_truth: Obviously this was before photography was invented, but many of these early telescopic astronomers did leave us drawings of their views of Jupiter: - Galileo Galilei left [these drawing from 1610 detailing the positions of Jupiter's moons](_URL_0_). Not much is seen of Jupiter itself other than a disc. - Robert Hooke, generally credited with discovering the Great Red Spot, had a better telescope and made [this drawing of Jupiter in 1666](_URL_2_). - Giovanni Cassini had a considerably better telescope than either. [Here are some of his drawings from 1665, 1672, and 1677.](_URL_1_)

Okay! Imagine you have a big, beautiful marble (that’s Jupiter) far, far away in the sky. In the 1600s, people who loved looking at the stars (called astronomers) had telescopes, but not as good as the ones we have now.

With their telescopes, they could see that Jupiter wasn’t just a tiny dot—it looked like a little round ball. They could also see that it had some little bright spots next to it! Those spots are actually Jupiter’s four biggest moons, but back then, people didn’t know that for sure—they just saw the spots.

They couldn’t see all the stripes and swirls on Jupiter like we can with our big, modern telescopes. So, they could see that Jupiter was bigger than a dot and had some friends (the moons) close by, but not all the pretty details we see today.

Think of it like looking at a picture of your pet from far away—you can tell it’s your pet, and maybe see if it has long ears, but you can’t see the tiny spots or the color of its fur very well. That’s how astronomers saw Jupiter in the 1600s!
